strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear empirical evidence (Figure 1) that cross-attention VLMs substantially underperform on fine-grained visual understanding tasks compared to token insertion
Simple and elegant core contribution: allowing text tokens to self-attend within cross-attention layers, creating implicit gating without architectural changes
Comprehensive experimental validation across 9 diverse benchmarks with both training from scratch and adaptation of pretrained models, demonstrating broad applicability

Thorough ablation studies, particularly Table 8's demonstration that masking self-attention severely degrades performance, combined with attention visualization (Figure 7) supporting the implicit gating mechanism
Significant performance improvements over standard cross-attention (10-20+ points on fine-grained tasks) while maintaining inference efficiency benefits
Practical efficiency analysis showing 74% training memory reduction and demonstrated application to streaming video captioning with constant memory overhead
Modular design allowing efficient adaptation of pretrained insertion-based models with only 352M-680M new parameters
Strong commitment to reproducibility with promised code/model release and extensive experimental details
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is a single modification to attention computation (Equation 2→3), appearing more as an engineering optimization than a fundamental advance in VLM design

Persistent performance gap to token insertion (~7% average, with gaps up to 13% on InfoVQA) without adequate investigation of why the fundamental gap remains, suggesting the core problem may not be fully addressed

Incomplete analysis of why text-to-text interaction specifically helps: the implicit gating explanation in Appendix A is somewhat hand-wavy, lacking rigorous justification for why self-attention creates effective gating

Training efficiency claims need qualification: Table 1 shows CASA training time (10h14m) is comparable to insertion (10h29m), and the comparison uses different model configurations (insertion reduced to 75% token limit), muddying practical advantages
CASA∨ variant shows 2-5% performance drops despite efficiency gains, limiting adoption when maximum efficiency is needed—insertion methods would be preferable in that scenario
Experimental setup concerns: insertion baselines use 75% of token limits and lower image resolution (672² vs 896²), making direct performance comparisons potentially confounded

Limited evaluation of streaming application: video captioning only compared to LiveCC (7B) baselines using a smaller 3B model; no comparison with other recent streaming approaches (e.g., StreamingVLM)
Missing ablations on hyperparameter sensitivity (local window size, number of CASA layers) and lack of analysis of what information flows through text-image vs. text-text attention
Implementation fragility suggested by footnote about FlashAttention-2 alignment constraints and potential edge cases with multiple images per window
No discussion of societal impacts, failure cases, or scenarios where CASA is inappropriate for deployment

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies and investigates why cross-attention VLMs underperform on fine-grained visual tasks (charts, documents, OCR)
Elegant and simple solution: enabling text self-attention in cross-attention layers is straightforward yet effective, facilitating adoption
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 9 benchmarks, multiple architectures, both training from scratch and adaptation scenarios, with solid baselines
Exceptionally thorough ablation studies: Table 8's masking experiments convincingly demonstrate self-attention importance; attention visualization provides interpretability
Strong practical demonstration: real-time streaming video captioning with constant memory cost while insertion-based methods OOM; comprehensive efficiency measurements
Technical soundness: proper use of Flash-Attention2, careful attention masking, detailed reproducibility specifications in appendix
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges ~7% gap to insertion, discusses trade-offs between variants, no overclaiming
Clear presentation: well-structured paper with informative figures and comprehensive appendix; logical progression from motivation to validation
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is a straightforward modification (add text self-attention to cross-attention) rather than a novel architectural insight
Evaluation fairness concerns: insertion baseline trained at lower resolution (672² vs 896²) and shorter sequences due to memory constraints, weakening performance gap claims
Persistent performance gaps on motivated benchmarks: InfoVQA (-13.2 pts), ChartQA (-8.2 pts) gaps undermine the stated goal of closing the insertion-based performance gap
Limited streaming video evaluation: only LiveSports3K tested with modest win-rate improvements (39.0% vs 33.7% for compressed insertion); lacks diversity
Local attention window constraints under-explored: text can only attend within image-delimited windows, limiting long-range dependencies across images; no failure mode analysis
Generalization concerns: only 2B and 3B models tested; scalability to other model sizes, vision encoders, and architectures unclear
Architectural design choices poorly justified: three variants without clear guidance on which to adopt; CASA∨ placement (every 4th layer) appears arbitrary
Insufficient failure analysis: no qualitative error analysis on high-gap benchmarks (InfoVQA, ChartQA); why self-attention helps specifically on fine-grained tasks unexplored
Incomplete design space exploration: Table 5 shows FFN updates help (+2 pts) but dismissed for cost; suggests potential improvements not investigated
Implicit gating mechanism lacks theoretical justification: empirically demonstrated but without principled explanation for why softmax over text+image tokens provides better gating than prior methods

strengths: Systematic and well-motivated decomposition of five key design differences (D1-D5) between cross-attention and token insertion, providing clear insights into efficiency-performance trade-offs
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple settings (from-scratch training on Helium1-2B and adaptation of pretrained Qwen2.5-VL) with extensive benchmarking on 9 diverse VLM tasks

Strong practical demonstration of streaming video captioning benefits: CA maintains near-constant memory and latency while token insertion models exhaust memory resources, addressing a real application need
Valuable empirical finding that prior CA underperformance stemmed from training pipeline differences rather than fundamental architectural limitations, effectively reframing the design space

Solid experimental methodology with detailed ablations, efficiency measurements (throughput, memory, FPS), comparisons to recent SotA baselines, and good reproducibility (detailed appendices, promised code release)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the paper primarily revisits an existing mechanism (CA from Flamingo 2022) with straightforward variant combinations (CA^∅, CA^<, CA^{t+v}); no novel architectural contributions presented

Significant unexplained performance gaps on important fine-grained understanding tasks (ChartQA: 4.2%, InfographicVQA: 3.5% drops) without sufficient investigation of root causes or whether these limitations are fundamental or fixable

Insufficient analysis of visual history compression mechanism (D5): the streaming setup relies on gist tokens to preserve multi-frame information from single-frame windows, but why and when this works remains unclear; Table 4 shows non-trivial performance gaps (e.g., NExT-QA: 64.8→60.5) that deserve deeper investigation

Training cost comparison incompletely specified: paper reports tokens/sec throughput but absolute training memory usage not clearly compared; sequence length/batch size trade-offs for insertion models (halved/doubled) complicate fair comparison
Parameter-sharing variant (CA^∅) shows efficiency gains but unexplained performance degradation; lacks analysis of whether this trade-off could be addressed through alternative designs
Limited investigation of failure modes and error analysis for document/chart tasks; missing ablation testing whether CA with full visual history would recover performance

Gist token design appears somewhat ad-hoc (reusing post-image delimiters); lacks principled justification and ablation studies on design choices; unclear how much visual information is actually preserved
Video evaluation scope limited to sports videos (LiveSports3K); generalization to other video domains and comparison fairness (3B vs 7B models with LiveCC) not fully addressed
